eat_a_red_apple_day.label: Eat a Red Apple Day
eat_a_red_apple_day.intro: A cheerful nudge to open December with something crisp: pick a red apple, polish it on your sleeve and enjoy the crunch. About as low-effort as a celebration can get.
funFacts: Botanists trace the cultivated apple back to wild trees in the Tian Shan mountains of Kazakhstan, where apple forests still grow.
Roughly a quarter of an apple's volume is air, which is why apples bob happily in a tub of water.
More than 7,500 apple cultivars exist worldwide, from tiny crab apples to varieties bred purely for cider.

mutt_day.label: National Mutt Day
mutt_day.intro: A day for mixed-breed dogs, the one-off characters whose ancestry is anybody's guess. It celebrates dogs that look like no other and nudges people towards the shelter.
funFacts: Mixed-breed dogs often benefit from hybrid vigour, the genetic advantage of drawing on a wider gene pool.
Laika, the first dog to orbit the Earth, was a mixed-breed stray picked up on the streets of Moscow.
The word mutt is short for muttonhead, an American insult from around 1900 that later softened into affection.

make_a_gift_day.label: Make a Gift Day
make_a_gift_day.intro: Three weeks before Christmas, this day suggests making a present instead of buying one. Baked, knitted, drawn or built: the point is that somebody spent time rather than money.
funFacts: Modern gift wrap was an accident: in 1917 the Hall brothers ran out of tissue and sold decorative envelope liners instead.
A Japanese furoshiki cloth wraps the gift and is reused afterwards, so the wrapping is part of the present.
Ribbon curls because the scissor blade stretches one side of the plastic more than the other, forcing it into a spiral.

cookie_day.label: National Cookie Day
cookie_day.intro: A whole day for the cookie in every form: crisp, chewy, iced or dunked in milk. December is the obvious slot, right in the middle of baking season.
funFacts: The day was launched in 1987 by the American bakery chain Blue Chip Cookies.
The word cookie comes from the Dutch koekje, little cake, and reached English through the Dutch settlers of New York.
In 2019 astronauts baked cookies aboard the International Space Station in an oven built for zero gravity.

day_of_the_ninja.label: Day of the Ninja
day_of_the_ninja.intro: An internet-born celebration of the ninja: black outfit, silent footsteps, throwing stars. Fans mark it by dressing up, watching ninja films and moving suspiciously quietly.
funFacts: Historical shinobi came mainly from the Iga and Kōga regions of Japan and worked as scouts, spies and saboteurs.
The all-black outfit comes from kabuki theatre, where audiences agreed to treat stagehands dressed in black as invisible.
Iga in Mie Prefecture runs a ninja museum with revolving walls and trapdoors, plus an annual ninja festival.

microwave_oven_day.label: National Microwave Oven Day
microwave_oven_day.intro: A salute to the humble box that turns leftovers into dinner in ninety seconds. Few kitchen appliances are mocked so often and used so relentlessly.
funFacts: Percy Spencer noticed in 1945 that a chocolate bar in his pocket melted while he stood beside an active radar magnetron.
The first commercial Radarange of 1947 stood nearly 1.8 metres tall, weighed around 340 kilograms and was water-cooled.
Household microwaves run at 2.45 gigahertz, a frequency that sets the water molecules in food spinning and warms it.

cotton_candy_day.label: National Cotton Candy Day
cotton_candy_day.intro: Spun sugar on a stick, mostly air and gone in seconds. The day honours a fairground classic that turns a spoonful of sugar into a cloud the size of a head.
funFacts: The spinning machine was patented in 1899 by the dentist William Morrison together with confectioner John C. Wharton.
Sold as Fairy Floss at the 1904 St. Louis World's Fair, it shifted more than 68,000 boxes at 25 cents each.
Germans call it Zuckerwatte, sugar wool, while the French order barbe à papa, meaning dad's beard.

brownie_day.label: National Brownie Day
brownie_day.intro: Dense, fudgy and stuck somewhere between cake and biscuit: the brownie gets its own December date. Whether the corner piece or the middle one wins remains unsettled.
funFacts: The brownie is credited to Chicago's Palmer House Hotel, which served a chocolate bar cake at the 1893 World's Fair.
The Brownies in the 1896 Boston Cooking-School Cook Book were made with molasses and contained no chocolate at all.
The Palmer House still bakes its version to the old recipe, finished with a glossy apricot glaze.

christmas_card_day.label: Christmas Card Day
christmas_card_day.intro: A nod to the first commercial Christmas card, printed in London in 1843. A good excuse to write a few lines by hand while everyone else is sending messages.
funFacts: Henry Cole commissioned the card because he had no time to answer his letters one by one; John Callcott Horsley drew it.
Around 1,000 copies were lithographed, coloured by hand and sold for a shilling each.
The design drew complaints because it showed a child being handed a glass of wine at the family table.

dewey_decimal_system_day.label: Dewey Decimal System Day
dewey_decimal_system_day.intro: The birthday of Melvil Dewey, born on 10 December 1851, whose numbering scheme still tells you where a book sits on the shelf. A quiet celebration of order among the stacks.
funFacts: Dewey published his classification anonymously in 1876 while working in the library of Amherst College.
The system splits all knowledge into ten main classes and then into tens again, so 796 lands you at sport.
Libraries in more than 130 countries use it, and it has been translated into over 30 languages.

tango_day.label: National Tango Day
tango_day.intro: Argentina celebrates the tango on the birthday of its most famous singer. Bandoneón, close embrace and a dance that turned a port-city sound into a world language.
funFacts: The date marks the birthday of singer Carlos Gardel in 1890 and of violinist Julio De Caro in 1899.
UNESCO added tango to its list of intangible cultural heritage in 2009, jointly for Argentina and Uruguay.
The bandoneón was built in Germany for chapel music long before it became the defining sound of Buenos Aires.

gingerbread_house_day.label: Gingerbread House Day
gingerbread_house_day.intro: A day for edible architecture: walls of spiced dough, icing as mortar and sweets on the roof. Structural failure is part of the fun.
funFacts: The custom took off in Germany after the Brothers Grimm published Hansel and Gretel with its witch's house in 1812.
Nuremberg's Lebkuchen bakers had their own guild, and the city's spiced cakes were traded right across Europe.
The largest gingerbread house on record, built in Texas in 2013, used around 3,000 kilograms of flour and 7,200 eggs.

violin_day.label: Violin Day
violin_day.intro: Four strings, a wooden box and a bow strung with horsehair. From concert halls to village fiddling, no instrument moves between worlds quite so easily.
funFacts: The violin took its familiar shape in 16th-century Cremona, where Andrea Amati built instruments that still survive.
A violin is assembled from around 70 separate pieces of wood, usually spruce for the top and maple for the back.
Antonio Stradivari is thought to have made about 1,100 instruments, of which roughly 650 still exist.

monkey_day.label: Monkey Day
monkey_day.intro: A day for monkeys and, loosely, all primates. It began as an art-school joke and grew into a fixture for zoos, illustrators and wildlife groups.
funFacts: Monkey Day was started in 2000 by the American art students Casey Sorrow and Eric Millikin.
Monkeys and apes differ mainly by the tail: monkeys usually have one, gorillas, chimpanzees and gibbons do not.
Japanese macaques in Jigokudani bathe in hot springs through the winter, a habit first observed in the 1960s.

cupcake_day.label: National Cupcake Day
cupcake_day.intro: One cake, one person, no knife required. The cupcake gets its December date, complete with swirled frosting and a fluted paper case.
funFacts: Amelia Simmons described a light cake baked in small cups in her 1796 book American Cookery.
Eliza Leslie printed a recipe called cup cake in 1828; the name most likely comes from measuring by the cup.
The 1-2-3-4 cake is named after its cups of butter, sugar and flour and the four eggs that go with them.

chocolate_covered_anything_day.label: National Chocolate Covered Anything Day
chocolate_covered_anything_day.intro: Strawberries, pretzels, crisps, coffee beans: if it holds still, it can be dipped. A day that treats chocolate as a coating rather than a food in its own right.
funFacts: Tempering gives chocolate shine and snap. Dark chocolate is often worked at 31–32 °C; milk and white chocolate need lower temperatures.
Enrobing machines replaced hand-dipping around 1900 and still pour a curtain of chocolate over passing sweets.
Japan has sold chocolate-coated potato crisps for decades, pairing salt with sugar long before it was fashionable.

wright_brothers_day.label: Wright Brothers Day
wright_brothers_day.intro: On 17 December 1903, the Wright brothers achieved the first powered, controlled and sustained airplane flights. Their first flight lasted twelve seconds: a short trip with an enormous place in aviation history.
funFacts: The first flight at Kill Devil Hills lasted 12 seconds and covered about 36 metres, the wingspan of a short-haul jet today.
The fourth attempt on the same day stayed up for 59 seconds and covered 260 metres.
Wilbur and Orville financed their experiments with the bicycle shop they ran in Dayton, Ohio.

i_love_honey_day.label: I Love Honey Day
i_love_honey_day.intro: A day for the jar at the back of the cupboard: honey, the only sweetener made by insects, stirred into tea, spread on bread or eaten straight off the spoon.
funFacts: For 500 grams of honey, bees visit around two million flowers and fly some 90,000 kilometres between them.
Honey keeps for a long time when properly stored in a tightly sealed container, but excess moisture can allow it to ferment.
A single worker bee produces about a twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in her entire life.

holly_day.label: Holly Day
holly_day.intro: A pun with a plant attached. The day celebrates holly, the glossy evergreen with spiny leaves and bright red berries that turns up on every winter wreath.
funFacts: Holly is dioecious: only female plants carry berries, and only if a male plant grows somewhere nearby.
The berries are mildly poisonous to people but see blackbirds and thrushes through the winter.
Lower leaves are spiky while the higher ones are often smooth, an adaptation against grazing animals.

cortado_day.label: National Cortado Day
cortado_day.intro: Espresso cut with an equal measure of warm milk: strong enough to taste, soft enough to drink slowly. A small glass with a large following.
funFacts: The name comes from the Spanish cortar, to cut, because the milk cuts the sharpness of the espresso.
In the United States it is often served in a Gibraltar, a small tumbler borrowed from a San Francisco café.
In the Basque Country the same drink is ordered as an ebaki, which means exactly the same thing.

crossword_puzzle_day.label: Crossword Puzzle Day
crossword_puzzle_day.intro: On 21 December 1913 a newspaper printed the first crossword, and a whole species of puzzle was born. Best marked with a pencil and one stubborn corner.
funFacts: Arthur Wynne's first word-cross appeared in the New York World in 1913 and was diamond-shaped rather than square.
The New York Times long dismissed crosswords as a waste of time and only began printing them in 1942.
In 1942 Britain's Daily Telegraph ran a crossword contest and quietly approached the fastest solvers for codebreaking.

mathematics_day.label: National Mathematics Day
mathematics_day.intro: India marks the birthday of Srinivasa Ramanujan, the self-taught mathematician who filled notebooks with results nobody could explain. A day for numbers and for curiosity.
funFacts: Ramanujan was born on 22 December 1887 and had almost no formal training in mathematics.
He left behind some 3,900 results, and mathematicians were still proving them decades after his death.
1729 is the smallest number expressible as the sum of two positive integer cubes in two different ways.

festivus.label: Festivus
festivus.intro: The holiday for the rest of us: no tree, no presents, just a bare aluminium pole and a chance to say out loud what annoyed you this year. Popularised on television, adopted in earnest.
funFacts: Festivus reached the world through the Seinfeld episode The Strike in 1997.
Writer Dan O'Keefe borrowed it from his own family; his father had celebrated a version of it since the 1960s.
The ritual has two parts: the Airing of Grievances at dinner and the Feats of Strength afterwards.

eggnog_day.label: National Eggnog Day
eggnog_day.intro: Eggs, cream, sugar, spice and usually a splash of something stronger. Eggnog gets its day at the height of the season, when the punch bowl is already out.
funFacts: Eggnog descends from posset, a medieval English drink of hot milk curdled with ale or wine.
One explanation for nog is the noggin, a small carved wooden cup once used for serving drinks.
Some eggnog recipes combine several spirits or fortified wines, such as rum, whiskey and sherry.

pumpkin_pie_day.label: National Pumpkin Pie Day
pumpkin_pie_day.intro: A slice of spiced pumpkin custard in a pastry shell, on a day when the oven is running anyway. Cinnamon, ginger and cloves do most of the work.
funFacts: Early European cooks hollowed out a pumpkin, filled it with spiced milk and baked the whole thing in the embers.
Amelia Simmons printed two pompkin pudding recipes in American Cookery in 1796.
Most tinned pumpkin sold in the United States is made from Dickinson squash rather than the orange carving type.

candy_cane_day.label: National Candy Cane Day
candy_cane_day.intro: Red and white, hooked at the top and impossible to eat quickly. The candy cane gets its day right after Christmas, while the tree is still full of them.
funFacts: They began as plain straight white sugar sticks; the hook and the red stripes only turn up around 1900.
A popular story credits a Cologne choirmaster in 1670 with the bent shape, though no contemporary source confirms it.
Bending the canes was hand work until Gregory Keller built a machine for the job in the 1950s.

cut_out_snowflakes_day.label: Make Cut Out Snowflakes Day
cut_out_snowflakes_day.intro: Fold the paper, snip a few notches, unfold and be surprised. A craft day for the quiet week between the years, and cheap decoration for every window.
funFacts: Real snow crystals grow six-fold because water molecules lock into a hexagonal lattice as they freeze.
Farmer Wilson Bentley photographed more than 5,000 snow crystals from 1885 onwards and never found two alike.
Folding the paper into six before cutting is the trick that makes a paper snowflake look like the real thing.

card_playing_day.label: National Card Playing Day
card_playing_day.intro: The days between Christmas and New Year were made for card games. Deal out a deck, argue about the rules and watch the afternoon disappear.
funFacts: Playing cards reached Europe in the late 14th century, most likely by way of Mamluk Egypt.
The French suits of hearts, diamonds, clubs and spades were cheap to stencil and pushed the older designs aside.
A shuffled deck of 52 cards has more possible orders than there are atoms making up the Earth.

tick_tock_day.label: Tick Tock Day
tick_tock_day.intro: Two days left in the year and a list of things still undone. Tick Tock Day is the friendly reminder to finish at least one of them before the clock runs out.
funFacts: Early mechanical clocks in medieval monasteries had no hands at all and simply rang a bell at the right hour.
The pendulum clock built by Christiaan Huygens in 1656 cut the daily error from about fifteen minutes to fifteen seconds.
A second is defined today by 9,192,631,770 oscillations of a caesium atom.

bacon_day.label: Bacon Day
bacon_day.intro: Crisp, salty and loud in the pan: bacon gets its own day just before New Year. Breakfast plate, burger topping or straight off the kitchen paper.
funFacts: The word bacon goes back to a Germanic root meaning back or ham and reached English through Old French.
British rashers are cut from the loin, while American streaky bacon comes from the fattier belly.
That smell in the pan is the Maillard reaction, the browning chemistry behind bread crusts and roasted coffee.

champagne_day.label: National Champagne Day
champagne_day.intro: The last day of the year is the one day when almost everyone reaches for the same bottle. Champagne gets its own date, cork included.
funFacts: A bottle holds around five bar of pressure, more than twice what a car tyre carries.
Dom Pérignon was a Benedictine cellar master who helped improve the quality of Champagne’s wines.
Physicist Gérard Liger-Belair calculated about a million bubbles rising through a single poured glass.
